figures.title: Visual Design Decision Process
figures.subtitle: Requirements Traceability Matrix – Logical Visualization
figures.primer: This drawing is the rule for every later design decision in the course. Conceptual inputs (RCAR) feed a Design Decision; the decision is only complete when it carries Justification + AMPRS. The red banner is not decoration: all design decisions are driven by the Conceptual Model.

objects.name: Red banner — Conceptual Model drives decisions
objects.what: Reminder printed above the flow: every Design Decision must be driven by the Conceptual Model.
objects.why: Stops product-first or example-first answers. If you cannot point back to RCAR evidence, the decision is not defendable.

objects.name: Conceptual column
objects.what: Left side of the drawing: Requirements, Constraints, Risks, Assumptions.
objects.why: These are inputs, not outputs. They exist before you pick a topology or product.

objects.name: Requirements
objects.what: What the solution must do or achieve (functional and non-functional).
objects.why: Primary driver into the Design Decision. No requirement means no justification for a capability.

objects.name: Constraints
objects.what: Boundaries you cannot change (existing fabric, budget, regulation, skills).
objects.why: Also drive the Design Decision directly. Constraints limit the solution space.

objects.name: Risks
objects.what: Conditions that could cause the design to miss requirements.
objects.why: Risks do not jump straight to a product choice; they feed Risk Mitigation.

objects.name: Assumptions
objects.what: Believed-true statements that are not yet validated.
objects.why: The drawing shows Assumptions feeding Risks. Unvalidated assumptions are a common root of design failure.

objects.name: Risk Mitigation
objects.what: Actions that reduce or handle identified risks.
objects.why: Sits between Risks and the Design Decision so mitigation is part of the decision, not an afterthought.

objects.name: Validate
objects.what: Proof step for assumptions and related claims before you lock the decision.
objects.why: Validation joins the same spine into the Design Decision. Guessing is not a decision.

objects.name: Design Decision
objects.what: The Logical output: the choice you will defend.
objects.why: It is the convergence point of Requirements, Constraints, Risk Mitigation, and Validate.

objects.name: Justification + AMPRS
objects.what: Every decision must include why it is correct and how it scores on Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability, Security.
objects.why: A choice without justification and AMPRS review is incomplete on this template.

objects.name: Logical column
objects.what: Right side: Design Decision and Justification + AMPRS.
objects.why: Separates evidence (Conceptual) from the choice you will implement (Logical).

facts: Conceptual inputs are Requirements, Constraints, Risks, Assumptions.
Assumptions feed Risks; Risks feed Risk Mitigation.
Requirements and Constraints point directly at the Design Decision.
Risk Mitigation and Validate join the spine into the Design Decision.
Design Decision produces Justification + AMPRS.
All decisions are driven by the Conceptual Model.

checks.stem: On this drawing, which side holds Requirements, Constraints, Risks, and Assumptions?
options: Logical column
Conceptual column
Only the AMPRS box
Only Risk Mitigation
checks.explanation: Those four RCAR boxes sit under Conceptual. Logical holds the Design Decision and Justification + AMPRS.
checks.reinforce: Re-read the left column header: Conceptual. Those boxes are inputs, not the decision itself.

checks.stem: According to the arrows on this drawing, what do Assumptions feed?
options: Design Decision directly, with no other step
Requirements
Risks
Modern Hardware
checks.explanation: The dotted relationship from Assumptions goes to Risks. Assumptions that prove false become risks to the design.
checks.reinforce: Find Assumptions at the bottom-left and follow the dotted arrow up to Risks.

checks.stem: What must sit with a Design Decision before the decision is complete on this template?
options: A preferred vendor quote only
Justification + AMPRS
A blank workbook row
An assumption that was never validated
checks.explanation: The Logical output is Design Decision leading into Justification + AMPRS. AMPRS is Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability, Security.
checks.reinforce: Look at the rightmost Logical boxes: Decision then Justification + AMPRS.

checks.stem: What does the red banner require for every design decision?
options: Drive the decision from the Conceptual Model
Drive the decision from the instructor demo
Drive the decision from the cheapest SKU
Drive the decision from a blank template
checks.explanation: The banner states that all design decisions are driven to / by the Conceptual Model — the RCAR evidence set.
checks.reinforce: Read the red line at the top of the slide before you leave this drawing.

figures.title: Business Initiatives Capability Map
figures.subtitle: RFS Future State Architecture: Mapping IT capabilities to business initiatives and priorities
figures.primer: This drawing is top-down: Business Initiatives → Use Cases → Services/Capabilities → Private Cloud Operating Model. It explains why VCF exists for Rainpole: technology is justified by business initiatives, not the reverse.

objects.name: Business initiative — Modernize Infrastructure
objects.what: Top-left initiative: modernize the infrastructure platform.
objects.why: Parent of on-prem private cloud, optimize ops, and extend to edge/public/sovereign clouds.

objects.name: Business initiative — Application Modernization
objects.what: Top-center initiative: modernize how apps are built and run.
objects.why: Parent of self-service for app teams, Kubernetes/modern apps, and Private AI apps.

objects.name: Business initiative — Security Modernization
objects.what: Top-right initiative: modernize security outcomes.
objects.why: Parent of compliance/hardening, lateral security/IDS-IPS, and faster ransomware/disaster recovery.

objects.name: Use case — Build/deploy private cloud on-premises
objects.what: Use case under Modernize Infrastructure.
objects.why: Direct driver for VCF as the private cloud foundation.

objects.name: Use case — Optimize infrastructure and operations
objects.what: Ops/efficiency use case under Modernize Infrastructure.
objects.why: Ties Day-2 operations and fleet practices to a business initiative.

objects.name: Use case — Extend DC to edge, public, sovereign clouds
objects.what: Hybrid/extension use case under Modernize Infrastructure.
objects.why: Shows the operating model is not only a single on-prem silo.

objects.name: Use case — Self-service for app teams
objects.what: Consumption use case under Application Modernization.
objects.why: Explains why Self-Service IaaS appears in the services layer.

objects.name: Use case — Kubernetes and modern apps
objects.what: Modern runtime use case under Application Modernization.
objects.why: Maps to Next Gen Apps capability.

objects.name: Use case — Private AI apps
objects.what: AI application use case under Application Modernization.
objects.why: Appears again as a named service/capability (Private AI).

objects.name: Use case — Compliance and harden infrastructure
objects.what: Security use case under Security Modernization.
objects.why: Business reason for governance and hardening controls later in design.

objects.name: Use case — Lateral security / intrusion prevention
objects.what: East-west security use case under Security Modernization.
objects.why: Justifies segmentation and detection capabilities in the platform.

objects.name: Use case — Accelerate ransomware/disaster recovery
objects.what: Recovery-speed use case under Security Modernization.
objects.why: Business driver for data protection and ransomware recovery capabilities.

objects.name: Services / Capabilities layer
objects.what: Self-Service IaaS, Legacy VM Apps, Next Gen Apps, Private AI, plus Service X/Y/Z placeholders.
objects.why: Many-to-many bridge: use cases consume services; services sit on one operating model.

objects.name: Private Cloud Operating Model (Service Factory, Service Operator)
objects.what: Bottom foundation spanning the whole map.
objects.why: All services depend on one operating model — not three disconnected silos.

facts: Hierarchy is Initiative → Use Case → Services/Capabilities → Operating Model.
Three initiatives: Modernize Infrastructure, Application Modernization, Security Modernization.
Each initiative has three use cases (nine total).
Services include Self-Service IaaS, Legacy VM Apps, Next Gen Apps, Private AI, and placeholders X/Y/Z.
Everything rests on the Private Cloud Operating Model (Service Factory, Service Operator).

checks.stem: What is the correct top-to-bottom order on this drawing?
options: Operating Model → Services → Use Cases → Business Initiatives
Business Initiatives → Use Cases → Services/Capabilities → Private Cloud Operating Model
Services → Business Initiatives → Hardware → Use Cases
Use Cases → Operating Model → Business Initiatives → Spines
checks.explanation: The map is business-first: initiatives on top, then use cases, then services, then the shared operating model.
checks.reinforce: Read the four horizontal bands from top to bottom on the slide.

checks.stem: Which three business initiatives appear at the top of this drawing?
options: Compute, Storage, Network
Modernize Infrastructure, Application Modernization, Security Modernization
Production, DMZ, Development
Spine, Leaf, Rack
checks.explanation: Those three initiative pills are the top band of the RFS future-state map.
checks.reinforce: Look at the three large rounded buttons across the top of the figure.

checks.stem: What does every service on this map sit on?
options: A separate operating model per silo
The Private Cloud Operating Model (Service Factory, Service Operator)
Only the Security Modernization initiative
Only dark-fibre DCI
checks.explanation: The bottom capsule is the shared Private Cloud Operating Model that underpins all listed services.
checks.reinforce: Find the long white bar at the bottom of the diagram.

checks.stem: Private AI appears in this drawing as:
options: Only a spine switch label
A use case under Application Modernization and a named service/capability
Only a storage array
Only an AMPRS score
checks.explanation: Private AI is both an Application Modernization use case and a service/capability oval.
checks.reinforce: Find Private AI in the use-case row and again in the services row.

figures.title: Current State: Independent vSphere Environments
figures.subtitle: Rainpole siloed Production, DMZ, and Development
figures.primer: This drawing is the as-is problem statement: three independent vSphere environments with dedicated vCenters. Storage is partly shared at the fabric layer for Prod/DMZ but arrays stay dedicated; Development is fully isolated. VCF design work starts from this siloed current state.

objects.name: Production environment (blue)
objects.what: Own vCenter, vSphere Cluster with VMs, and dedicated physical hosts.
objects.why: Shows production is a management and compute silo today.

objects.name: DMZ environment (yellow)
objects.what: Own vCenter, vSphere Cluster with VMs, and dedicated physical hosts.
objects.why: DMZ is intentionally separate for security posture, still independently managed.

objects.name: Development environment (green)
objects.what: Own vCenter, vSphere Cluster with VMs, and dedicated physical hosts.
objects.why: Dev is a third management silo, not a cluster under production vCenter.

objects.name: Dedicated vCenter per environment
objects.what: Three separate vCenter instances — one above each cluster.
objects.why: There is no single management plane across Prod/DMZ/Dev in current state.

objects.name: vSphere Cluster + hosts per environment
objects.what: Each environment has its own cluster box and host icons beneath it.
objects.why: Compute is not shared across the three environments in this drawing.

objects.name: Prod/DMZ FC Fabric (shared)
objects.what: One horizontal Fibre Channel fabric bar spanning Production and DMZ.
objects.why: Connectivity is shared between Prod and DMZ — but that is not the same as shared arrays.

objects.name: Dev FC Fabric (dedicated)
objects.what: Separate shorter FC fabric bar under Development only.
objects.why: Development storage networking is isolated from Prod/DMZ.

objects.name: Dedicated storage arrays under Prod/DMZ fabric
objects.what: Two separate disk stacks under the shared Prod/DMZ fabric.
objects.why: Shared fabric, dedicated arrays — data-at-rest stays per environment.

objects.name: Dedicated Dev storage array
objects.what: One disk stack under the Dev FC fabric.
objects.why: Dev has both its own fabric and its own array.

facts: Three environments: Production, DMZ, Development.
Each environment has a dedicated vCenter.
Prod/DMZ share an FC fabric but use dedicated arrays each.
Development has dedicated FC fabric and dedicated array.
Current state is siloed management and mostly siloed storage.

checks.stem: How many vCenter instances does this current-state drawing show?
options: One shared vCenter for all three environments
Two vCenters (Prod+DMZ shared, Dev separate)
Three — one dedicated vCenter per environment
None — hosts are managed only by NSX
checks.explanation: Each vertical environment block has its own vCenter at the top. Management is siloed.
checks.reinforce: Count the vCenter boxes above Production, DMZ, and Development.

checks.stem: What is true about Prod and DMZ storage in this drawing?
options: They share one array and one fabric
They share an FC fabric but keep dedicated storage arrays
They have no storage shown
They use only local vSAN with no fabric bar
checks.explanation: The callout and diagram show a shared Prod/DMZ FC fabric with separate array stacks underneath.
checks.reinforce: Read the Prod/DMZ fabric bar, then count the two array stacks under it.

checks.stem: How is Development storage drawn relative to Prod/DMZ?
options: Fully shared fabric and shared array with production
Dedicated FC fabric and dedicated storage array
Shared fabric with Prod but no array of its own
Only object storage with no FC fabric
checks.explanation: Dev has its own fabric bar and its own array stack — full storage isolation in current state.
checks.reinforce: Compare the short Dev FC Fabric bar and single Dev array to the Prod/DMZ side.

checks.stem: What problem does this drawing establish for a VCF design?
options: Already one consolidated private-cloud operating model
Independent siloed vSphere environments that a future-state design must address
A finished stretched cluster across Albany
That BGP is unsupported on the underlay
checks.explanation: The slide is titled Current State: Independent vSphere Environments — three silos with dedicated management.
checks.reinforce: Hold this drawing against the Business Initiatives map: silos today vs one operating model tomorrow.

figures.title: Current State: Data Center Topology
figures.subtitle: Rainpole San Jose L3 spine-leaf fabric and DCI latencies
figures.primer: This drawing is the physical underlay you must read before networking design decisions. San Jose is L3 spine-leaf, dual-homed leaves to dual spines, VXLAN-capable, with OSPF and BGP. DCI uses redundant dark fibre: 25 ms to Salt Lake and 80 ms to Albany — numbers that matter for sync vs async site design.

objects.name: San Jose DC
objects.what: The data center this fabric drawing represents.
objects.why: Site context for all leaf/spine and DCI statements on the slide.

objects.name: Spine01
objects.what: One of two spine switches at the core of the L3 fabric.
objects.why: Every leaf uplinks to both spines for fabric redundancy.

objects.name: Spine02
objects.what: Second spine switch, peer to Spine01.
objects.why: Dual-spine design; a single spine would be a fabric SPOF in this model.

objects.name: Leaf01–Leaf06 and Leaf-n
objects.what: Top-of-rack / leaf switches; drawn in pairs per rack, with Leaf-n showing scale-out.
objects.why: Leaves are where racks attach; they dual-home to both spines.

objects.name: Rack 1, Rack 2, Rack 3, Rack n
objects.what: Rack groupings under leaf pairs, with server icons in each rack.
objects.why: Shows multi-rack scale and that the pattern repeats to Rack n.

objects.name: Servers dual-homed to rack leaves
objects.what: Hosts in a rack connect to both leaves in that rack.
objects.why: Host NIC redundancy is to the leaf pair, not directly to the spines.

objects.name: Leaf-to-both-spines uplinks
objects.what: Lines from each leaf to Spine01 and Spine02.
objects.why: Classic L3 spine-leaf: east-west via spines, redundant paths.

objects.name: L3 Spine-and-Leaf architecture (callout)
objects.what: Text states Rainpole fabric is L3 spine-leaf.
objects.why: This is the underlay model VCF overlay expects; it is usually a retain-and-validate constraint.

objects.name: OSPF and BGP supported
objects.what: Routing protocols called out for in-fabric and outside connectivity.
objects.why: BGP matters later for NSX Edge uplinks; OSPF/BGP show the fabric is a routed L3 design.

objects.name: VXLAN-capable fabric
objects.what: Callout that the physical fabric can carry VXLAN.
objects.why: Underlay readiness signal for overlay designs (still must prove MTU/path).

objects.name: DCI — redundant dark fibre
objects.what: San Jose interconnects to other DCs over redundant dark fibre.
objects.why: Physical site coupling exists; latency numbers decide sync options.

objects.name: Latency to Salt Lake — 25 ms
objects.what: Stated DCI latency from San Jose to Salt Lake.
objects.why: Far above typical sync vSAN/site limits (~5 ms RTT). Treat as async/backup territory unless other evidence appears.

objects.name: Latency to Albany — 80 ms
objects.what: Stated DCI latency from San Jose to Albany.
objects.why: Even higher latency — not a sync stretch candidate from this drawing alone.

facts: Architecture is L3 spine-leaf at San Jose DC.
Two spines: Spine01 and Spine02.
Leaves dual-home to both spines; servers dual-home to rack leaf pairs.
OSPF and BGP are supported; fabric is VXLAN-capable.
DCI via redundant dark fibre: 25 ms to Salt Lake, 80 ms to Albany.

checks.stem: What underlay architecture does this drawing show for San Jose?
options: Layer 2 stretched campus with a single core
L3 Spine-and-Leaf
Hub-and-spoke WAN only
Server-to-spine direct attach with no leaves
checks.explanation: The callout and the Spine01/02 + Leaf01…n drawing are classic L3 spine-leaf.
checks.reinforce: Read the first bullet on the right and match it to the spine/leaf icons.

checks.stem: How do leaf switches connect to the spines in this drawing?
options: Each leaf connects to only one spine
Each leaf dual-homes to Spine01 and Spine02
Leaves connect only to other leaves, never to spines
Only Rack 1 leaves connect to spines
checks.explanation: The mesh of lines shows every leaf uplinking to both spines.
checks.reinforce: Trace lines from Leaf01 upward — they reach both Spine01 and Spine02.

checks.stem: Which statements does the slide assert about protocols and overlay readiness?
options: Only static routing; not VXLAN-capable
OSPF and BGP supported; fabric is VXLAN-capable
BGP only to Albany; no OSPF; no VXLAN
AppleTalk and IPX; Geneve only on spines
checks.explanation: Right-side bullets list OSPF and BGP support and that the physical fabric is VXLAN-capable.
checks.reinforce: Read bullets 2 and 3 on the right panel.

checks.stem: From this drawing alone, what do the Salt Lake (25 ms) and Albany (80 ms) figures imply for sync site designs?
options: Both sites are within a typical 5 ms sync RTT budget
Latencies are far above typical sync limits, so sync stretch is not supported by these numbers
80 ms is fine for sync; 25 ms is not
Latency is irrelevant because dark fibre is redundant
checks.explanation: 25 ms and 80 ms are well above common synchronous cross-site limits. Redundant dark fibre is not the same as sync-capable latency.
checks.reinforce: Read the DCI bullet: redundant dark fibre plus the two latency numbers. Keep those for later stretch questions.

figures.title: Logical Design Template
figures.subtitle: Modern Private Cloud Capability map
figures.primer: This drawing is the target logical capability map. Consumers sit above integrations; consumption/services, operations, and virtualized infrastructure stack in the center; security and data-protection pillars run the sides; modern hardware is the base. Use it to place every later design decision in the correct layer.

objects.name: Multi-Tenant Consumers — LOBs, Devs/SREs, Platform Teams
objects.what: Top dotted box with three consumer personas.
objects.why: Design starts from who consumes the platform, not from a SKU.

objects.name: Integrations and 3rd Party Ecosystem
objects.what: Full-width bar under consumers.
objects.why: External tools and partners plug in above the private-cloud stack.

objects.name: Consumption and Services
objects.what: Self-Service Portal; API|CLI|CI/CD; Infra-as-Code; Data/App Runtime/AI-ML/LBaaS services; IaaS|CaaS|PaaS|XaaS bar.
objects.why: How users request and run services — distinct from Operations.

objects.name: Operations
objects.what: Fleet management, Performance Optimization, Visibility/Observability, Analytics/Reporting, Cost Efficiency, Capacity, Configuration Management.
objects.why: Day-2 control plane capabilities live here, not in the consumer pills.

objects.name: Virtualized Infrastructure — Compute, Storage, Network
objects.what: Bottom center triad on which higher services run.
objects.why: Classic VI layer; still above Modern Hardware.

objects.name: Security Governance and Compliance pillar
objects.what: Identity/RBAC, Auditing/SIEM, Constraint-Based Management, Data Governance, Compliance Enforcement.
objects.why: Cross-cutting left pillar — not a single product box in the center stack.

objects.name: Data Protection and Recovery pillar
objects.what: Data Protection, Disaster Recovery, Disaster Avoidance, Ransomware Recovery.
objects.why: Cross-cutting right pillar for resilience and recovery outcomes.

objects.name: Modern Hardware
objects.what: Foundation bar under the entire stack.
objects.why: Physical substrate; logical capabilities sit above it.

objects.name: IaaS | CaaS | PaaS | XaaS
objects.what: Service delivery models inside Consumption and Services.
objects.why: Names the consumption models the platform must offer.

facts: Consumers: LOBs, Devs and SREs, Platform Teams.
Center stack: Consumption and Services → Operations → Virtualized Infrastructure.
Side pillars: Security Governance and Compliance; Data Protection and Recovery.
Base: Modern Hardware.
Consumption includes IaaS|CaaS|PaaS|XaaS and self-service/API/IaC entry points.

checks.stem: Which personas appear in the Multi-Tenant Consumers box?
options: Spine01, Leaf01, Rack 1
LOBs, Devs and SREs, Platform Teams
Only Production and DMZ

checks.explanation: The top dotted region lists LOBs, Devs and SREs, and Platform Teams.
checks.reinforce: Read the three black pills at the top of the template.

checks.stem: Where do Fleet management and Capacity Management belong on this template?
options: In the Operations band
In Modern Hardware only
In the consumer pills

checks.explanation: Those capabilities are drawn inside the Operations section of the center stack.
checks.reinforce: Find the Operations band (gauge icon) and read its green/teal buttons.

checks.stem: Identity and RBAC appears in which part of the drawing?
options: Virtualized Infrastructure next to Storage

Only under Modern Hardware

checks.explanation: Identity and RBAC is the top item in the left Security Governance and Compliance pillar.
checks.reinforce: Scan the left shield pillar from top to bottom.

checks.stem: What sits directly under Virtualized Infrastructure (Compute/Storage/Network) on this template?
options: Business Initiatives
Modern Hardware
Assumptions
Leaf-n only
checks.explanation: The black foundation bar is Modern Hardware — the physical base of the capability map.
checks.reinforce: Look at the bottom-most bar inside the main grey container.
